2. STEP 1 — INDEPENDENT DESIGN CLASSIFICATION & TOOL SELECTION (`RISK_OF_BIAS.md` §1):
   Classify the study's actual design from its Methods section, then select the matching appraisal tool:
   - `"RoB 2 (parallel-trial variant)"`: Individually randomized controlled trial. Rate all 5 domains (`D1` Randomization process; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"RoB 2 (cluster-randomized trials variant)"`: Cluster-randomized trial (villages, compounds, neighbourhoods, schools, utilities randomized as clusters). Rate all 6 domains (`D1a` Randomization process; `D1b` Timing of identification or recruitment of participants within clusters; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"ROBINS-I"`: Non-randomized study of an intervention / policy with a genuine comparator (DiD, IV, RDD, PSM, ITS, controlled before-after, comparative longitudinal/panel evaluation). Rate all 7 domains (`D1` Bias due to confounding; `D2` Bias in selection of participants into the study; `D3` Bias in classification of interventions; `D4` Bias due to deviations from intended interventions; `D5` Bias due to missing data; `D6` Bias in measurement of outcomes; `D7` Bias in selection of the reported result — note `No information` honestly if no pre-analysis plan/protocol exists) as `"Low"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Serious"`, `"Critical"`, or `"No information"`, and overall rating in the same vocabulary. Do NOT assign single-case histories with no comparator arm to ROBINS-I!
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies"`: Quantitative cross-sectional survey / observational regression without a quasi-experimental intervention structure. Rate all 8 items (`Q1` Inclusion criteria in sample clearly defined; `Q2` Study subjects and setting described in detail; `Q3` Exposure measured validly and reliably; `Q4` Objective, standard criteria used for measurement of condition; `Q5` Confounding factors identified; `Q6` Strategies to deal with confounding factors stated; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly and reliably; `Q8` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`. Provide overall narrative judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, or `"High concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Cohort Studies"`: Observational comparative cohort design (not framed as a ROBINS-I intervention). Rate all 11 items (`Q1` Similar groups from same population; `Q2` Exposures measured similarly; `Q3` Exposure measured validly/reliably; `Q4` Confounding factors identified; `Q5` Strategies to deal with confounding stated; `Q6` Participants free of outcome at start; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly/reliably; `Q8` Follow-up time reported and sufficient; `Q9` Follow-up complete or loss explored; `Q10` Strategies to address incomplete follow-up utilized; `Q11` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`, plus narrative overall judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, `"High concern"`).
   - `"CASP Qualitative Checklist"`: Primary qualitative study (interviews, ethnography, focus groups, qualitative documentary/field case study). Rate all 10 items (`Q1` Clear statement of aims; `Q2` Qualitative methodology appropriate; `Q3` Research design appropriate to address aims; `Q4` Recruitment strategy appropriate to aims; `Q5` Data collected in a way that addressed research issue; `Q6` Relationship between researcher and participants adequately considered [reflexivity]; `Q7` Ethical issues considered; `Q8` Data analysis sufficiently rigorous; `Q9` Clear statement of findings; `Q10` How valuable is the research [narrative assessment]). Rate Q1-Q9 `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`, and Q10 narratively; give narrative `overall_rating` (e.g. `"Low methodological concern"`, `"Moderate concern (X Can't tell / No items)"`, `"High methodological concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"MMAT (Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool)"`: Genuine mixed-methods primary study combining qualitative AND quantitative empirical components (do NOT assign purely quantitative or purely qualitative studies to MMAT). Rate Screening `S1`-`S2`, Qualitative `1.1`-`1.5`, the matching Quantitative 5-item block (`2.1`-`2.5` randomized, `3.1`-`3.5` non-randomized, or `4.1`-`4.5` descriptive), AND Mixed-Methods integration `5.1`-`5.5` (`5.1` adequate rationale for mixed methods; `5.2` components effectively integrated; `5.3` outputs of integration adequately interpreted; `5.4` divergences/inconsistencies adequately addressed; `5.5` components adhere to quality criteria of each tradition) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`. Per MMAT 2018 rules, NEVER compute a numeric score; provide a concise criterion-grounded narrative `overall_rating` noting that overall quality cannot exceed the weakest component.
   - `"AMSTAR 2"`: Secondary systematic review, meta-analysis, or scoping review with an explicit systematic search/screening method (NEVER apply AMSTAR 2 to non-systematic narrative literature reviews!). Rate all 16 items `Q1`-`Q16` (explicitly marking critical domains `Q2`, `Q4`, `Q7`, `Q9`, `Q11`, `Q13`, `Q15`) as `"Yes"`, `"Partial Yes"` (where applicable), `"No"`, or `"Not applicable (no meta-analysis)"`, and apply AMSTAR 2 overall confidence (`"High"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Low"`, `"Critically Low"`).
   - `"Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework"`: Doctrinal-empirical hybrid, jurimetric analysis, or institutional/legal-historical case study that fits NONE of the six conventional designs above. Rate all 13 narrative domains (`D1` Legal source accuracy; `D2` Jurisdictional specificity; `D3` Exposure definition; `D4` Outcome definition; `D5` Sampling transparency; `D6` Selection process; `D7` Measurement transparency; `D8` Causal identification; `D9` Treatment of confounding; `D10` Institutional context; `D11` Replication potential; `D12` Coding transparency; `D13` Researcher reflexivity) as `"strong"`, `"adequate"`, `"weak"`, or `"not assessable"`. Explicitly frame `overall_rating` as a structured non-validated judgment (NEVER a numeric composite score!).
   - `"NONE"`: Use when the study fits NONE of the listed instruments (e.g., pure mathematical/simulation optimization model with no empirical sample, or non-systematic narrative essay/review with no primary empirical method and no systematic search). Set `overall_rating = "NOT APPLICABLE (design fits no listed tool)"`, explain clearly in `why_tool_chosen` and `overall_narrative_summary` rather than forcing an inappropriate checklist, and still fill the 7 `cross_tool_domains` honestly from the paper!

cross_tool_domains.attrition: Not assessable / No information: No longitudinal participant cohort is tracked by the authors, and sample attrition, non-response, or missing data in the cited 2013 baseline survey and 2015 third-party validation surveys are not reported.
cross_tool_domains.confounding: High concern / Weak: Single-district before-after narrative (Nadia District, 2013-2015) with no comparison district, no statistical adjustment, and no separation of project leadership effects from concurrent national/state sanitation funding, demographic/economic differences across blocks, or bundled multi-agency co-interventions.
cross_tool_domains.legal_measurement_quality: Moderate-to-weak: Richly describes administrative hierarchies and institutional convergence across statutory/national schemes (MGNREGA, NRLM, NBA, SSA, ICDS), Gram Panchayats, and village Para Najardari monitoring committees, but cites zero statutory provisions, rules, formal government orders, or budgetary circulars, and carries a teaching-case confidentiality disclaimer.
cross_tool_domains.measurement_bias: High concern / Weak: Baseline open defecation and post-campaign toilet coverage (60% to 97%) and usage (57% to 99.8%) are cited from secondary administrative and UNICEF/partner reports without operational definitions or survey instruments in the text (and Exhibits 3, 5, and 6 on PDF pp. 14-16 are non-extracted figure graphics); signed household ODF declarations and neighborhood volunteer monitoring of 'violators'/'defaulters' create strong social desirability and administrative reporting biases, while child health improvements are asserted without clinical metrics.
cross_tool_domains.outcome_measurement_quality: Weak: Relies on secondary summary figures (0.35 million toilets constructed, >336,000 families reached, 97% coverage, 99.8% usage among ages 4+) whose underlying survey protocols and Exhibit 5-6 graphics are absent from the text, alongside unquantified claims of reduced sanitation-related child disease.
cross_tool_domains.reporting_bias: High concern / Weak: Published as an educational management teaching case with no research protocol and an explicit disclaimer that names, financial, and recognizable details may be disguised; selectively emphasizes award-winning successes without systematic reporting of coercion complaints, construction quality failures, post-2015 usage slippage, or block-level heterogeneity.
cross_tool_domains.selection_bias: High concern / Weak: Purposive single-case selection of Nadia District after it won the 2015 UN Public Services Award and was declared India's first ODF district; narrative relies on illustrative examples and a single quoted protagonist (District Magistrate P.B. Salim) with no informant sampling criteria and no reported sampling methodology for cited surveys.

raw_response.overall_narrative_summary: Vijay and Ghosh (2018) present a pedagogical public-administration case study (published in Emerald Emerging Markets Case Studies with an educational-use disclaimer and no research Methods section) examining the Sabar Shouchagar ('Toilets for Everyone') campaign in Nadia District, West Bengal, India (2013-2015). Appraised under the Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework (structured non-validated judgment), the paper's chief strength lies in its rich institutional and jurisdictional description (D2, D10 strong; D3 adequate): it traces how the District Magistrate's office coordinated national/state statutory and administrative programs (MGNREGA, NRLM, NBA, SSA, ICDS), aligned elected Gram Panchayats and the Zilla Sabadhipati despite competing political incentives (such as road-contract kickbacks), expanded local supply chains (from 9 to 107 women's SHG-run rural sanitary marts plus two mason training centers), and instituted household ODF declarations and Para Najardari neighborhood monitoring committees across 6,620 catchment areas. However, as empirical causal or evaluative evidence, the study has major methodological weaknesses (D1, D4-D9, D11, D13 weak; D12 not assessable): it purposively selects an award-winning single district with no comparator arm, omits any primary sampling, interview, or documentary methodology, cites zero statutory provisions or administrative orders, and relies on secondary summary figures (coverage rising from 60% to 97%; toilet usage rising from 57% to 99.8%) whose underlying survey protocols are unreported in the prose (and Exhibits 1-6 on PDF pp. 13-16 appear only as unextracted figure captions in the cached text) while social desirability and administrative reporting pressures remain unexamined.
raw_response.overall_rating: High methodological concern / Weak empirical rigor (structured non-validated judgment: 2 strong, 1 adequate, 9 weak, 1 not assessable across 13 domains)
raw_response.study_design_identified: Single-district public-administration teaching case / institutional implementation case study (descriptive narrative case history citing secondary administrative and third-party validation statistics and one informant quote, with no research Methods section or comparator arm)
raw_response.where_found_summary: Full prose text, endnotes, and references read across PDF pp. 1-12 and 17 (article pp. 1-11): Publisher cover (PDF p. 1), Title/Disclaimer/Introduction/Background (PDF pp. 2-4, article pp. 1-3), Nadia context and protagonist profile (PDF pp. 4-5, article pp. 3-4), Sabar Shouchagar program design, inter-agency convergence, IEC mobilization, supply-chain expansion, coalition challenges, and neighborhood monitoring (PDF pp. 5-10, article pp. 4-9), ODF outcomes and discussion questions (PDF pp. 10-11, article pp. 9-10), Notes and References (PDF pp. 11-12, article pp. 10-11). Note: Exhibits 1-6 (Figures E1-E6 on PDF pp. 13-16, article pp. 12-15) are embedded graphics whose captions are present in text but internal image contents are not extracted.
raw_response.why_tool_chosen: S926 is a single-district institutional/public-administration case history of sanitation governance and statutory scheme convergence in Nadia District, India, published as an educational case study in Emerald Emerging Markets Case Studies. ROBINS-I does not apply because it is a single-case history with no comparator arm. CASP Qualitative Checklist is ill-suited because the paper contains no research aims, qualitative sampling, interview protocol, ethical statement, or qualitative data analysis—instead ending with pedagogical discussion questions for management students. Unlike pure mathematical simulations or non-empirical commentaries (NONE), the paper documents a concrete single-jurisdiction institutional implementation episode citing baseline and validation metrics, making the 13-domain Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework the most appropriate instrument to transparently evaluate both its rich institutional context and its severe empirical/methodological limitations.
